title: Smartsheet’s new AI tool tracks corporate strategies, suggests fixes
summary: Work management software vendor Smartsheet has launched a new tool to help executives oversee company-wide strategies, with AI agents that monitor progress, identify problems, and recommend fixes. vsActual, announced Wednesday at Smartsheet’s Engage event, is a standalone “AI-native” application, separate from the company’s core work management software. It pulls data from a variety of business applications, including Oracle, Salesforce, SAP, and Workday, as well as work management tools such as Smartsheet itself. vsActual uses AI agents that carry out tasks on behalf of users, either in response to natural language prompts or running automatically in the background. An intake agent uses existing documents, such as presentation decks and spreadsheets, to help create a “plan of record” that includes goals, timelines, and budget and capacity limits. A planning agent helps with capacity planning and scenario modelling, and can be invoked when a plan needs to change. A drift agent can continuously look for data that highlights problems such as budget overruns, schedule delays, and resource conflicts. To do this, vsActual analyzes information from a range of connected applications, including conversations in Slack. vsActual agents can also recommend corrective actions, such as allocating additional staff to a project to address a predicted delay. Smartsheet Other agents include a data quality agent and a reporting agent that keeps users up to date on any changes across projects. “vsActual is aimed at the C-Suite, specifically the CFO and COO, who are often battling the issue of budget creep and timeline drift,” said Liz Miller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research. Tracking the gap between strategies and actual outcomes — a concept that Smartsheet describes as “execution drift” — is a common challenge for executive teams, said Miller, and is typically only revealed in PowerPoint slides during quarterly planning sessions, or via emailed Excel spr

title: HP’s next CEO loves confrontation
summary: The new year will see a new CEO for HP, which after a nine-month search has named Emma Walmsley to lead the company from January 4, 2027. Walmsley was previously CEO of drug company GSK, where she turned around its finances and spun off its consumer healthcare business into a new company, Haleon. She has a reputation for courting confrontation rather than yes-men in the boardroom . HP needs a shake-up as revenue from printing declines and AI-driven demand for components is forcing up PC prices. She will take over from HP’s interim CEO Bruce Broussard, who stepped in in February when former CEO Enrique Lores left the company after more than 25 years to become president and CEO at PayPal. There’s a consolation prize for Broussard, who will become chair of HP’s board, succeeding Chip Bergh who remains a board member. Although Walmsley has been on Microsoft’s board for seven years (she is stepping down in December), this is her first foray into leading a tech company. Her almost 16-year tenure at GSK included more than eight years as CEO, and earlier in her career, she spent 17 years at L’Oréal. Bergh said that during the executive search, she stood out “for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth.” He particularly cited her people-first leadership approach. Walmsley reiterated her commitment to the philosophy in a post on LinkedIn . “HP has an extraordinary innovation heritage, an inspiring purpose and an incredible opportunity ahead as AI reshapes technology and what customers need from it. I’m excited to build on those strengths and help translate innovation into impact,” she wrote. “Behind every innovation are the people who work to make someone’s day a little easier, their work more productive, their ideas possible. In an age of AI, I believe human leadership has never mattered more. It’s a privilege to be joining this team.” Announcing

title: How to get early access to Android’s smart new scam shield
summary: When it comes to Android security , we’ve got three main types of threats to contend with as informed phone-owners determined to keep our data safe. First, there are the theft-related worries — the breaches that happen when someone physically takes possession of your device and manages to get past its virtual gates. (Setting up Android’s native theft protection options and enabling all the right Android security settings in advance makes a massive difference in terms of proactive protection.) Next, there are the many, many theoretical threats played up by companies hoping to sell you over-the-top security software. (Choosing a device that actually gets timely and reliable software updates and then maintaining a teensy shred of common sense is generally all that’s needed to keep these overhyped boogeymen at bay.) And finally, every single one of us faces the most worrisome threats of all — the ones related to good old-fashioned trickery and our own occasional lapses in judgment. From phishing to smishing and vishing and now even quishing (I swear I’m not making these up), there’s no shortage of shenanigans trying to trick us into willingly giving up our information without even realizing it. And all the easily accessible AI these days only makes matters worse . Suffice it to say, that last category is generally the most pressing — ’cause it’s our own very human shortcomings that make it possible. And even the most savvy and cautious creatures among us can be convinced to click a thoroughly cloaked questionable link in the right moment. With that kind of threat, your best bet is simply having as many layers of protection as possible in front of you — so if your own guard is ever down and a particularly convincing scam attempt appears in front of you, there’ll be something standing between it and you that says: “Hey buddy: You sure you want to do this?” That’s precisely what’s popping up as an easily overlooked new option on Android right now — in one of the places whe

title: Apple VP Tom Boger on MacBook Pro weight, design, and the return of the glowing logo
summary: Almost everyone in tech already knows about Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, a light, bright, thin pro Mac notebook with a reference-grade touch responsive display, adding a touch of iPad to the Mac. It’s already being talked about as the future, at least of the company’s pro laptops. I spoke with Apple’s Vice President of Mac and iPad Product Marketing, Tom Boger, to find out more. The specs of the new MacBook Pro are written about everywhere — including here — so I wanted to get a feel for how Apple thought about building the system. We looked at the weight the team took out, the restraint behind its design choices, the illuminated logo it brought back, and why the Mac makes so much sense for the enterprise. Weight: a thousand small decisions The first thing people notice about the new MacBook Pro, Boger said, is how much lighter it has become. The 14-inch model is about half a pound lighter, and the 16-inch about 0.7 pounds lighter. This weight loss was not easy to achieve. The team looked at every single component used in the Mac to find opportunities to reduce its weight, Boger said. “It’s not one thing here, one thing there. It’s a thousand things.” The challenge is to reduce the weight of individual components while leaving each part as functional as it was. “You have to make sure you’re not compromising the integrity of whatever component you’re taking the weight out of.” I pictured engineers shaving away microns, milligrams, and grams from all the components used. “That’s literally what it takes,” Boger said. Of all the things Apple did with this product, he said, this was probably the one where “you really have to sweat every little detail.” Design: raise the bar, don’t change the Mac The display is the headline feature of this MacBook Pro, Boger said. title: AWS launches Kiro bots to help devs coordinate AI coding agents
summary: AWS on Thursday launched Kiro bots, generally available within Kiro Crew, its open-source multi-agent development environment, to help developers coordinate parallel coding tasks, maintain context across sessions, and automate recurring software development workflows. Kiro bots are designed to take responsibility for specific parts of a developer’s workflow rather than execute isolated tasks within individual agent sessions, in turn addressing the growing coordination burden developers face as they increasingly rely on multiple AI agents to handle software development tasks in parallel, AWS said in a statement. Setting up bots and how do they work Developers can create a bot by opening the Customize section in Kiro Crew and selecting the “Add a bot” option, where they can choose either a default agent or an existing custom agent as its foundation. Each bot can be assigned a specific responsibility, such as issue triage, build monitoring, or release readiness, and customized with its own name, avatar, instructions, tools, and permissions based on the tasks it is expected to handle, the hyperscaler said. Developers can use each bot to launch multiple worker-agent sessions in parallel and have it monitor their progress, redirect those that deviate from the plan, and consolidate their results. If a task requires their input or a decision, the bot can seek their approval while continuing with other tasks that do not depend on it, it added. To maintain continuity across sessions, each bot also maintains its own persistent memory through a feature AWS calls Notes. These Notes capture a bot’s understanding of projects, including developer preferences, previously made decisions, project requirements, and constraints gathered through its work and feedback from developers. The accumulated context helps each bot apply the same instructions and judgment to subsequent tasks without developers having to repeatedly explain their expectations, the hyperscaler said. Its cloud service will become read-only on November 13 before shutting down on November 20, when Conductor will begin deleting cloud user data. Existing customers can transfer their cloud workspaces to the local application or export their data. The local version will continue receiving new AI models and critical bug fixes until early 2027, when it will begin winding down. Conductor said it would delete user data when the application shuts down. Meta’s strategy for AI coding Conductor could help Meta establish itself as a provider of AI development platforms rather than competing solely through its own models , according to Lian Jye Su , chief analyst at Omdia. “The most important differentiator of Conductor is it sits above individual coding agents,” Su said, adding that he expects Meta to maintain its model-agnostic approach. That would allow developers to continue working with different AI coding systems through a common interface, although Meta has not disclosed whether Conductor’s existing integrations will be retained in the product planned for next year. title: Why enterprise AI needs unified metadata infrastructure
summary: Enterprise AI has produced a lot of noise about models, GPUs, vector databases, and agent frameworks. Those conversations matter. But the shift that will decide whether enterprise AI works is happening underneath the models. For decades, metadata meant documentation. Teams built catalogs so people could find data sets, governance programs recorded definitions and ownership, and lineage helped reconstruct what broke, after it broke. Metadata described the business. AI expects metadata to run it. That gap is bigger than it sounds. An AI system doesn’t inherit the years of institutional knowledge a senior analyst holds in their head. It doesn’t know that finance’s definition of revenue excludes returns while sales’ definition includes them. It doesn’t know a customer ID became unreliable after a migration three years ago. It doesn’t know churn got redefined last quarter. People pick that up over time, usually by getting burned once. AI simply answers using whatever definition it happens to land on, with no burned-once memory to fall back on. That’s what turns metadata from documentation into infrastructure. Business meaning is now infrastructure Infrastructure is anything every application depends on without thinking about it: the network, identity, storage. Every application assumes it exists. Business meaning belongs on that list now too. Every AI application depends on the same definitions of customer, revenue, product, contract, and risk holding steady across systems. When they don’t, AI scales the inconsistency faster than any team of humans ever could. BI showed us this problem first. Two dashboards would return two different numbers because two tools implemented the same metric two different ways. Most organizations learned to live with it: reconciliation meetings, spreadsheet showdowns, a standing argument about whose report is right. AI broke the tolerance for semantic inconsistency. title: Your LLM writes good SQL. That’s not the same as safe SQL
summary: A few years into working with data, I’ve learned that the hardest part of an AI system is rarely the model. Usually it’s the question of who gets to ask what. That question came up for me while building an LLM analytics tool on Snowflake Cortex for healthcare engagement and field-performance data. The tool let people ask questions in plain English, and it cut recurring analytics turnaround from days to minutes. It also made me realize that a fast, accurate answer can still be the wrong answer. A correct query can still be the wrong one Most of us test text-to-SQL the same way. We ask a question, check that the query runs, and compare the output to what we expected. That works right up until the answer is correct for the wrong person. Picture a sales rep who types “quarterly sales for my hospitals” and gets every hospital in the region back. The SQL is clean. The result is still a problem, and the same thing can happen in a multi-tenant app, an HR system, or a finance tool. Start with who is asking The first change I’d make is to what the model is allowed to see. Before anything is generated, look up who is asking: their role, business unit, territory, and assigned accounts. Then give the model only the tables and columns that person can use. Sensitive fields such as customer IDs, contract terms, or salaries should be tagged in your metadata catalog so they are never offered in the first place. It sounds obvious, but it is easy to skip when a demo is working. A prompt is not a permission system It is tempting to add “only show my territory” to the system prompt and move on. I understand the appeal. But a prompt is a suggestion, and the model can ignore it, forget it, or misread it on a hard question. A better setup parses the generated SQL and rewrites it before anything runs, so the rules live in code that the model cannot talk its way around.
